finding: The $120 floor of the live range looks about right. The $1,025 ceiling is higher than anything we could build for one sensor on these four examples, but one benchmark does reach it, so it is wide at the top without being clearly wrong. Built totals for one upstream sensor (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2020 Subaru Impreza about $145-$551 ($84.95 house-brand sensor to $358.75 Subaru list, 0.5-1.2 hr); midsize 2020 Subaru Outback 2.5L up to about $502 ($310.42 Subaru list, 1.2 hr), low end not built because no aftermarket upstream sensor price for this car could be found; truck 2016 F-150 3.5L EcoBoost about $128-$327 ($68.10-$166.98, 0.5-1.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $194-$566 ($133.82 Bosch to $406.30 BMW list, 0.5-1.0 hr). The bottom: the lowest total, $128, is an aftermarket sensor at an online price plus a 0.5 hour warranty time, so $120 sits at or just under the supportable floor. The top: the highest built total is about $566. RepairPal ($440-$523), ConsumerAffairs ($200-$500) and Jerry ($159-$247 typical, $600-$800 for premium models or hard-to-reach sensors) all stop well short of $1,025. YourMechanic's Subaru Outback page is the exception: its mobile quotes for one upstream sensor on the six-cylinder Outback are $636-$649 and it gives shop/dealer prices of $745-$1,075 for those same jobs. So a figure near $1,000 is something a dealer may quote for one sensor on a six-cylinder or hard-to-reach engine, but most single-sensor jobs on four-cylinder cars build to roughly $130-$570. A total near the top can also mean two sensors replaced together, a seized sensor needing thread repair, or a labor rate well above $160 an hour. How solid the labor times are: two are manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicles, Ford's 0.5 hour (right) and 0.6 hour (left) for the F-150 3.5L EcoBoost including reading the codes, and Subaru's 1.2 hours (front) and 1.0 hour (rear) for the Impreza and Outback. The Subaru time is longer than the general 30 to 60 minute figure, so for those two classes the manufacturer time is the high end and the general figure the low end. The BMW hours are a general statement only; BMW bulletins refer dealers to BMW's own labor system instead of printing a time. Jerry's guide gives a similar general figure (0.5-0.8 hour for an easy-reach sensor, 1.5-2.0 hours or more for a hidden one). Because five of the eight hour figures are general and not for the example vehicle, and the Outback has no aftermarket price, the confidence is low. What is weak or missing: the Outback low end is null (the retailer page for the 2020 car sells only downstream sensors); the Impreza and BMW low ends are a retailer house brand and a Bosch part, and no Denso or NTK price could be loaded for either; the F-150 still rests on one priced page; and the Outback's former dealer-site price ($273.25, a different part number) is no longer used. Upstream versus downstream: the upstream sensor (an air/fuel ratio or wideband sensor on most newer cars) is the dearer part and the one priced in the classes. Downstream sensors seen: Subaru genuine $232.85 list against $358.75 (Impreza) or $310.42 (Outback) upstream, aftermarket $31.95 against $84.95, with a 1.0 hour rear time against 1.2 front; F-150 genuine rear $138.91 list and aftermarket $34.06-$65.34; BMW $325.06 list against $406.30, Bosch $122.32 against $133.82. A Nissan bulletin (NTB22-007A, 2013-2016 Altima 2.5L and Sentra, rear sensor warranty extension) allows 0.3 hour for the voltage check and 1.3 hours for the readiness drive pattern but prints no separate replacement time. Honda and Acura bulletins that replace an air/fuel sensor together with a catalytic converter (1.3-2.4 hours combined) were not used because the sensor time cannot be separated out.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or code-scan fee (a sensor code can also be caused by an exhaust leak, wiring fault, vacuum leak or a failing catalytic converter, so the sensor is not always the fix), shop supplies and sales tax. V engines have two upstream and two downstream sensors, and a shop may recommend replacing a pair. A sensor seized in the exhaust can add labor or thread repair. Some repairs finish with a drive cycle to reset the emissions readiness monitors, which may be billed as extra time.
